rv.q: This was not the trickery of surface caricature but the mystery of deep acting at work.
Ian McKellen and Patrick Stewart find plenty of consoling comedy in two masterpieces of existential despair.

What makes this 'Godot' special is that Messrs. McKellen and Stewart, in addition to being consummate stage actors, are also close friends whose mutual affection illuminates every moment of their lengthy exchanges.
These shows are an irresistible celebration of two actors’ love affairs with their scripts.
The stars behind Magneto and Charles Xavier go head-to-head again and light up Broadway in Harold Pinter’s “No Man’s Land” and Samuel Beckett’s “Waiting for Godot.”
If you have to pick one, “No Man’s Land” is the way to go.
But, while there is much to enjoy in the production, I felt I was watching talented comic performers rather than listening to the still sad music of humanity.
Both Land and Godot, in fact, prove that the most challenging and unsettling material can make for accessible, even buoyant, entertainment.
McKellen and Stewart bring their considerable star power and decades of theatrical experience to Beckett's masterpiece, creating a production that feels both timeless and immediate.

It is, nevertheless, sheer folly to build a revival of Godot, one of the most challenging plays in twentieth-century drama, on a pair of actors with little theatrical experience and limited technical skills.
Director Sean Mathias has staged, almost choreographed, a dazzling cast in a haunting performance of a poignant, classic play.

cn.t: McKellen and Stewart's star power and real-life friendship elevate this revival, mining humor and pathos from Beckett's masterpiece, though some critics find the production too cosy and question whether celebrity casting overshadows the play's bleaker essence.
